title: Beyond Episodic AI: Cognitive Field Networks for Biologically Inspired Persistent Cognition
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 15 Sep 2026]
    Title:Beyond Episodic AI: Cognitive Field Networks for Biologically Inspired Persistent Cognition
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Cognitive Field Theory (CFT) proposes that cognition arises from memory-dressed collective dynamics that generate a persistent macroscopic cognitive field. Here we develop a Cognitive Field Network (CFN), a recurrent Transformer in which the organized hidden field re-enters subsequent inference through \[ \Phi_{n+1}=F_{\theta}(X_{n+1},\Phi_n). \] Rather than prescribing an explicit memory operation, the CFN allows new information to act on an already history-dependent collective state. We find that learning organizes persistent, content-dependent recurrent dynamics whose timescale increases systematically with the trained recurrent horizon. Semantic continuation propagates the recurrent state far beyond this horizon without replay of the target answer. Without content-specific support, the field exhibits finite passive relaxation, whereas periodic re-exposure to relevant input repeatedly renews the surviving state and drives it toward an approximately stationary nonzero regime. Unrelated-input and recurrence-off controls do not reproduce this behavior, while near-paraphrased re-exposure produces weaker renewal, demonstrating representation-sensitive persistence. These results distinguish three dynamical processes: collective memory dressing forms and sustains a history-dependent cognitive field, structured input reorganizes this field, and cross-cycle re-entry makes the resulting state causally available to subsequent inference. The CFN therefore provides a controlled computational platform for studying persistent, history-dependent cognitive dynamics without a separately prescribed memory system.

report.summary: A new recurrent Transformer, the Cognitive Field Network, sustains persistent history-dependent cognition by re-entering a collective hidden field across inference cycles without an explicit memory system.
report.background: Large language models are powerful but largely episodic: they reason within a bounded context window and forget once it closes. Efforts to fix this usually bolt on external memory, such as retrieval-augmented generation, vector databases, or hand-designed memory tokens. State-space models and recurrent architectures offer another route, but still define memory as an explicit mechanism. Cognitive Field Theory takes a different stance, arguing that cognition emerges from collective neural dynamics that produce a persistent macroscopic field. This paper builds a computational version of that idea, a Cognitive Field Network, and tests whether persistence can arise from learned recurrent dynamics alone rather than from a prescribed memory operation, positioning the work between neuroscience-inspired theory and practical sequence modeling.
key_points: The Cognitive Field Network replaces explicit memory modules with a recurrent hidden state, or field, fed back into every new inference step. Learning organizes this state into content-dependent dynamics whose memory timescale grows with the recurrent horizon used in training. Memory becomes an emergent property of the dynamics instead of a designed component.

The field outlives its training horizon. In semantic continuation tests the recurrent state keeps propagating the original context well past the trained horizon, without replaying the target answer. This suggests the network carries forward meaning, not just a cached token sequence.

Persistence requires support. Without content-specific input the field relaxes passively and fades, but periodic re-exposure to relevant material renews the surviving state and drives it toward an approximately stationary, nonzero regime. Unrelated input and recurrence-off controls do not reproduce this, so persistence is content-sensitive.

Paraphrased re-exposure produces weaker renewal than near-identical input, showing the field is representation-sensitive rather than a generic buffer. The authors separate three processes: memory dressing forms the field, structured input reorganizes it, and cross-cycle re-entry makes the resulting state causally available to later inference.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the work points toward architectures where long-term coherence comes from dynamics rather than ever-larger context windows or external retrieval stacks, potentially reshaping how agents, assistants, and continual-learning systems are built. Developers get a controlled platform to study persistent recurrent state, an alternative to attention-only memory designs, and new evaluation questions around horizon and re-exposure. Regular users could eventually see assistants that remember and refine context across sessions instead of resetting each conversation, with more natural long-horizon collaboration. The same persistence raises privacy and control concerns, since a surviving cognitive field may retain traces of past interactions in ways that are harder to inspect, edit, or delete than a conventional stored memory.
report.tools: To follow up, watch the paper's experimental code and any Hugging Face or GitHub release. Related open-source work includes Transformer-XL and Compressive Transformer for recurrent memory, Recurrent Memory Transformer implementations, and state-space models such as Mamba and RWKV in the Hugging Face Transformers ecosystem. For the biological side, Dynamic Field Theory toolkits and Nengo offer ways to model persistent fields. Also track alphaXiv and Connected Papers for follow-on citations.
